clue.text: Crusading movement is back, with alarm spreading around in next to no time

indicators.note: the brief span of time is placed on either side, wrapping the jumbled letters
letters that spread out lose their order and are laid down afresh

parts.note: taken as written
a moment is an instant, next to no time at all
the rear is the back of something

explanation.surface: A crusade returns, sounding a hasty alarm that spreads in an instant.
explanation.walkthrough: Moral Re-Armament was a mid-20th-century international movement campaigning for moral and spiritual renewal; 'is' is only a link here.
explanation.definitionFit: Moral Re-Armament was an evangelising international organisation, aptly described as campaigning with missionary zeal.

clue.text: First-class Scottish town, one displaced by English

indicators.note: something displaced is pushed out of its spot so another thing can take it over

parts.note: Stirling is a town in central Scotland
the Roman numeral for one
standard abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: A top-class Scottish town loses out to an English rival.
explanation.walkthrough: Take STIRLING and swap its I for E.
explanation.definitionFit: Sterling as an adjective means of excellent quality, thoroughly reliable and worthy.

clue.text: Dairy product consumed by Muffet apparently

indicators.note: what is consumed by something ends up inside it, so look within the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Little Miss Muffet ate curds and whey, so a dairy food seems a fair guess for her meal.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Little Miss Muffet sat on a tuffet eating her curds and whey, which makes 'apparently' sound like a comment on her diet.
explanation.definitionFit: Feta is a crumbly Greek cheese made from sheep's or goat's milk, a typical milk-based food.

clue.text: Description of Brutus by Caesar just before his death in bare feet?

definitions.text: Description of Brutus by Caesar just before his death
definitions.meaning: first meaning: Shakespeare's Caesar asks 'Doth not Brutus ... kneel?' moments before being stabbed, using an old word for in vain
second meaning, taken literally: having no boots on

explanation.walkthrough: In Julius Caesar, Act 3, Caesar's last speech includes 'Doth not Brutus bootless kneel?', meaning kneeling to no purpose; the question mark flags the jokey literal reading.
explanation.definitionFit: The archaic adjective means unavailing or futile, while its literal parts describe someone with no footwear on.

clue.text: Member in non-drinking organisation right off beer?

indicators.note: the limb sits inside the abstinence group, surrounded by its letters

parts.note: Alcoholics Anonymous, a fellowship of people who abstain from alcohol
a leg is a limb, or member, of the body
standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A teetotal group member is right to give up beer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'right off beer' reads like a pledge to quit drinking, but 'off beer' is ale that has gone sour; alegar is malt vinegar, from ale plus French aigre, sour.
explanation.definitionFit: Alegar is vinegar made from ale, so it is literally beer that has soured and gone bad.

clue.text: Singers and actors given position on scale — all but "no good"

parts.note: the cast is the set of actors in a production

indicators.note: all but means everything except, so the abbreviation for no good is removed

parts.note: a rating is a position on a graded scale
NG is the abbreviation for no good

explanation.surface: Singers and actors are ranked on a scale where nothing comes out as no good.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Position on scale' suggests a musical note, but it is a rating, which loses its N and G.
explanation.definitionFit: Castrati were male singers castrated before puberty to keep a soprano or alto voice, prized in baroque opera.

clue.text: Unoriginal dish includes fish? On the contrary

indicators.note: one thing includes another by holding it inside
this swaps the roles just stated, so the holder becomes the thing held

parts.note: the cod is a common food fish
a pie is a baked dish

explanation.surface: A dull, derivative recipe: a dish with fish in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Read straight, the pie holds the fish; 'On the contrary' reverses that, so the fish wraps round the pie.
explanation.definitionFit: Something copied is reproduced from another's work, so it lacks originality.

clue.text: Saluting a foe, one reintegrated into worldwide community

indicators.note: reintegrated means put back together in a new form, so the letters are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: the letters of all four words

explanation.surface: Greeting a former enemy, one nation is welcomed back into the world community.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface evokes postwar reconciliation, fitting the body set up after the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: The League of Nations was the international body founded in 1920 to keep peace among states, forerunner of the UN.

clue.text: Bubbly cream may ease pain here?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: bubbling, as boiling water does
second meaning, taken literally: ointment applied to a painful skin abscess

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bubbly cream' reads as a frothy cosmetic, but the clue splits after the first word; a boil is a pus-filled swelling on the skin.
explanation.definitionFit: Something on the boil is bubbling hot, or figuratively active and lively; literally, ointment goes onto a skin swelling.

clue.text: Greatly admire ace illustrator

parts.note: A is the card abbreviation for ace
Gustave Doré, the 19th-century French engraver famed for his Bible and Dante illustrations

explanation.surface: Someone is full of praise for a brilliant illustrator.
explanation.definitionFit: To adore is to love or worship someone, a stronger form of admiration.

clue.text: A point made about old railway network needing to be up-to-date

indicators.note: something made about another is built around it, enclosing it

parts.note: taken as written
east is a point of the compass
British Rail, the UK's nationalised railway until the 1990s

explanation.surface: Someone argues the old railway system needs modernising.
explanation.walkthrough: British Rail ran the UK's trains until privatisation in the 1990s, hence 'old'.
explanation.definitionFit: To keep abreast of something is to stay informed and current with it, fully up-to-date.

clue.text: Focus of Bach's work that's given minimal coverage?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the instrument string on which the famous Air arrangement is played
second meaning: a skimpy piece of underwear

explanation.walkthrough: Bach's 'Air on the G String' is the popular name for an arrangement of his Orchestral Suite No 3 movement, played on a violin's lowest string.
explanation.definitionFit: The violin's lowest string carries the Air arrangement, and the same name is used for a tiny garment covering very little.

clue.text: Sally is girl needing a head transplant

indicators.note: a transplant swaps one organ for another, so the first letter is changed for a new one

parts.note: a maid is an old word for a girl or young woman

explanation.surface: A woman called Sally needs a serious operation.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not say which letter becomes the new head, so the crossings settle it: MAID becomes RAID. 'Sally' looks like a name but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sally is a sudden attack or sortie by troops, much like a raid on an enemy position.

clue.text: A hiker out to get ride possibly — man in a cap?

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or wrong, so the preceding letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of both words

indicators.note: possibly hints at one of several arrangements of the word it follows

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A walker heads out to hitch a lift, perhaps a man in a flat cap.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Hardie, the Scottish founder of the Labour Party, famously arrived at Parliament in 1892 wearing a working man's cloth cap rather than a top hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Hardie's cloth cap became his trademark, so he is a famous example of a man known for that headgear.

clue.text: Lager is drunk — port, too

indicators.note: someone drunk is unsteady and muddled, so these letters are scrambled

parts.note: the letters of both words

explanation.surface: Beer is drunk, and port as well: quite a session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' looks like the fortified wine in a drinking scene, but it is a harbour city.
explanation.definitionFit: Algiers, capital of Algeria, is a major Mediterranean seaport on the North African coast.

clue.text: English paper boys to be without round in the near future Gadzooks!

definitions.note: Gadzooks! flags that the word is archaic

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the boys sit around the ring shape

parts.note: standard abbreviation for English
the Financial Times newspaper
sons are boys
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: An English newspaper's paperboys will soon be out of a delivery round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' here means outside, as in old usage. Gadzooks! is a mock-old oath, telling the solver the answer is equally antique.
explanation.definitionFit: Eftsoons is an archaic adverb meaning soon afterwards or presently, so it points to time shortly ahead.

clue.text: Official to feel unwell, having got hit about

indicators.note: the blow goes about, or around, the word for feeling poorly

parts.note: biff is informal for a punch or blow
to ail is to be ill

explanation.surface: A functionary feels poorly after being punched.
explanation.definitionFit: A bailiff is a court officer who enforces judgments, serving writs and seizing goods.

clue.text: Bound to see the end, but not the very end

indicators.note: the very end is the final letter, which is dropped

parts.note: to behold is to see
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone is determined to watch to the finish, though not quite the last moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound to' reads as 'certain to', but 'Bound' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Beholden means under obligation or indebted to someone, tied to them by a debt of gratitude.

clue.text: I beat incoming supporter up as quick as anything!

indicators.note: coming in means entering the middle of the other words

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word for the supporter is written bottom to top

parts.note: a fan is a supporter
to lash is to beat or whip

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of thrashing an arriving fan in no time.
explanation.walkthrough: The supporter goes between I and LASH.
explanation.definitionFit: In a flash is an idiom for instantly, extremely quickly, like a burst of light.

clue.text: A street, ornate, in dull European city

indicators.note: the first three items are placed inside the word for dull

parts.note: mat, a variant spelling of matt, describes a dull, non-glossy finish
taken as written
standard abbreviation for street
rich decoration is ornate

explanation.surface: A fancy street stands out in an otherwise drab European city.
explanation.walkthrough: The insertion goes after the second letter of the outer word, not in its exact centre.
explanation.definitionFit: Maastricht is a city in the southern Netherlands, known for the 1992 treaty creating the EU.

clue.text: One of the same clan with name cast in stone

indicators.note: something cast in stone is embedded within it

parts.note: agate is a banded semi-precious stone
standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A clan member's name is set in stone for posterity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast in stone' sounds like an idiom for permanence, but here it places the letter inside the gem.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnate is a relative descended through the male line from a common ancestor, a kinsman.

clue.text: Pub had food provided from the very start

parts.note: an inn is a pub
ate means had food

explanation.surface: The pub served food right from opening.
explanation.definitionFit: Innate qualities are inborn, present in someone since birth rather than acquired later.

clue.text: Senile state associated with repetition

parts.note: GA is the postal abbreviation for Georgia, a US state
the abbreviation for the state, said again

explanation.surface: Doddering old age is linked with saying things twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Senile state' reads as one phrase, but it splits: 'Senile' defines and 'state' is the American state.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaga is an informal adjective for someone confused or doddery through old age.

clue.text: Sun disappearing? There's a wind from the southwest

parts.note: once Sunday has gone, Monday's short form comes next
the question mark asks what comes when: shortly afterwards

explanation.surface: The sun goes in, and a southwesterly gale blows up.
explanation.walkthrough: Sun is the abbreviation for Sunday, not the star: when Sunday is disappearing, Mon is soon, written as one word.
explanation.definitionFit: The monsoon is the seasonal wind of South Asia, blowing from the southwest in summer and bringing heavy rain.

clue.text: Attractive female given garland — learning to take the lead

parts.note: lore is accumulated knowledge or learning
a lei is a Hawaiian flower garland

explanation.surface: A beautiful woman is presented with a flower garland at a ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Garland' comes first in the clue, but 'to take the lead' sends the knowledge word to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: The Lorelei is the Rhine siren whose beauty and song lured boatmen to their deaths, an alluring woman.

clue.text: Regretted being offensive in speech

indicators.note: in speech means as the words are spoken, so go by the pronunciation

parts.note: rude means offensive or impolite

explanation.surface: Someone regrets having been rude in a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: To rue something is to feel sorrow or remorse over it, so rued is past regret.

clue.text: It's impracticable whichever way you look at it

indicators.text: whichever way you look at it
indicators.note: looking from either direction gives the same result, so the letters read identically both ways

parts.note: the phrase meaning this reads the same left to right as right to left

explanation.surface: Someone declares an idea unworkable from every angle.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying a plan is not on is a British idiom meaning it cannot be done or is unacceptable.

clue.text: The people here when functioning in a series of social events

parts.note: these points to people or things here
as can mean when, as in 'as I left'
a machine that is on is functioning

explanation.surface: The guests here are active on the social circuit.
explanation.walkthrough: The Season is the annual round of British upper-class social events such as Ascot, Henley and debutante balls.
explanation.definitionFit: The London Season is the traditional summer calendar of balls, races and parties for high society.
